en: May that left or right side of the Bull-bannered Lord, who has half his body as a woman, bring you glory— He who bears upon His forehead a mark branded by the crest of fire, wears over His ear an expanding playful earring, possesses the luster of a neck as white as the moon born from the ocean, and bears a chest covered by the slough of a serpent. (Kalhaṇa, *Ardhanārīśvarastotra*, 1)

May that Lord of Gaurī bring you joy— he upon whose lap Guha slowly settled after a long time, recognizing him with the words, "This is my mother," as his left eye was still anointed with collyrium, his throat appeared darkened from the direction of the south, a mirror rested in his hand, and the moon was situated in his crown.

"Release his deer-skin; pearls suited for the tips of breasts have been cast into the hollow of his skull. What need is there for collyrium from the fire on his forehead? Therefore, [use it] for the sake of your eyes.

While the Goddess was thus attempting to dissuade the Lord regarding the joining of the two halves of his body, may Hara—who, even while being restrained by his beloved, remained intent on pursuing her reply—protect you.

Victorious is the creation of the body of the Lord, fashioned from the female and male portions of a beautiful woman, which serves as a treasury of attainable excellence through its two-fold composition: a bow constructed from the tips of a goat’s and a cow’s horns, and likewise a host of attendants formed from the halves of the bodies of Naraka and Karati.

"This is not the greatness of asceticism consisting of eating leaves and wind; behold these two, the bull and the serpent, who have now been made to subsist on nothing but external elements for that very reason.

Thus, while hearing from the mouth of Aparṇā—herself free from pride—these words pleasing to the ear, which were spoken by the celestial nymphs out of love for this half of the Teacher of the Moving and the Stationary, [the bull spoke].

May that Goddess protect you—she whose delight in these [serpents] is like that of a male cuckoo for the hair of snakes; whose eye, seeing before her, rejoices at the rays of light from the throat-region of the male cuckoo;
and whose tongue, throbbing separately, utters such speech which, though consisting of similar syllables, has distinct meanings, as the two blessed ones join together in a fresh mutual union.
The left hand desires to apply collyrium to the right eye, while the right arm seeks to fasten a serpent-bracelet upon the left;
thus may the face of the Blessed One—marked by a shared smile as He gazes upon His two halves, each unaware of its own role—grant you the fulfillment of your heart's desire.

"May there be for you the auspiciousness of a firm embrace; may there be well-being for you, and enough with these endearments! What more shall we say? You are indeed worthy of trust after your playful quarrel with your beloved.

While this was being said, as long as [the couple] remained with their virtues made apprehensive by their intense separation, may that very moment of union between Śiva and Śivā be for your supreme welfare. 8.
May that crest-jewel of Ardhanārīśvara—the half of which is the moon—be for your prosperity;
it creates the illusion of being a second portion exceeding the face of the Mountain’s Daughter.
May the body of Śiva, which has merged with the form of the Daughter of the Mountain—thereby transcending its own distinctness—dispel all misfortunes for you here without obstacle;
for there, his body shines as if embraced by the form of his beloved, encircled by the braid of her serpent-wife whose dark luster is as curved as a serpent’s body. 10 [RT 4.1]

May that Pārvatī, the inner sanctum of the Teacher of the mobile and immobile world, who knows the practice of virtuous conduct, shatter all evil—she who, though her entire retinue was excluded from half the dwelling by the Blessed One, remained steadfast; for there were only mature chamberlains, an aged bull, a hunchback, and the moon, her eternally trusted companion. 11 [RT 8.1]

May the inconceivable body of Śiva and Śivā grant you well-being—that body which wanders at will through pleasure gardens, forests, and cremation grounds; which is sometimes fully clothed and sometimes naked; which is both modest and shameless; and which possesses the great splendor of incomparable beauty in its form as Bhairava. (12)
Like the light of the crescent moon, it is slightly closed like a window for the Fortune of the world; it is frequented by the faces of the princes, which resemble bees, as if to drink its beauty;

and because of its height, it is perfumed by the breath from mouths and made fragrant for the sense of smell—for whom, then, would this lotus of the chest of Śiva and Gaurī not bring delight to the mind? (13)

May that eye of the two Lords protect the world— half of it lovely and charming, and half of it smeared by the blazing fire— situated in the place of the forehead-mark (tilaka), upon seeing which the god Smara simultaneously becomes both arrogant and despondent as he attempts with his moon-crest to hold a bow in his palm for the act of play.
The serpent feeds on air, the bull, afflicted by hunger, grazes upon grass, and the man without even a loincloth strives to support his family; yet I am overwhelmed by anxiety because of poverty.
Salutation to that one who, appearing in the form of Gaurīśvara, made a single morsel of food for him, and who is the bestower of desired fruits to the three worlds. 15.

We praise that madman, the soldier of Love, who deafens the quarters with the twang of his bowstring, repeatedly brandishes his arms, boasts of himself by himself, and raises his threatening forefinger most loftily—all this because he considers himself a hero when the Lord of the Half-Woman (Śiva) was born merely from the impetuosity of his sport. 16.

In the body of the Daughter of the Mountain King there dwells a fragment; on his crest is a fragment of the moon; and the Lord himself, the wielder of the broken-axe (Khaṇḍaparaśu), is himself a fragment.
Nevertheless, the unfragmented activity of the Lord toward one who has newly sought refuge triumphs in this world through compassion. (17) [= SKA 15.37]

May that Blessed Lord Ardhanārīśvara grant us the realization of non-duality—he upon whose head the moon, mingled with the night of the Daughter of the Mountain’s braid, remains joined with half of his body, having made it appear as if severed in order to follow his Lord out of love. 18 [ŚRT 1.1.2]
